newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua ex-contras release government hostages.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua ex-contras release government hostages.

text.p: Former contra rebels have released eight members of a government peace commission who were kidnapped while on a mission to seek the rebels' surrender, a Nicaraguan army spokesman said on Tuesday.
Despite army reports of the kidnapping throughout the day, the Nicaraguan government late on Tuesday denied that it ever took place.
"There was a kidnapping, but they (in the government) don't want to admit it because they were able to resolve it today," one army source told Reuters on condition of anonymity.

The rebels, part of the Northern Front 3-80 group active in Nicaragua's northern mountains, had planned to disarm and return to civilian life on Tuesday, in accordance with a peace pact signed last month.
Instead, the army said, they took eight members of the government commission hostage at dawn on Tuesday in the village of Kuskawaas, about 150 miles (250 km) north of the capital Managua.

But the government, through its newly formed Defence Ministry, denied the kidnapping took place, pointing to the first outward sign of friction between the armed forces and President Arnoldo Aleman, who took power early this year.
"There is not now nor has there existed a kidnapping," Jose Adan Guerra, the deputy defence minister, told a news conference.
The army, however, stood by its story, saying the hostages were released on Tuesday afternoon about 12 hours after being seized.
Those captured included two Defence Ministry officials, one journalist and five members of the Special Disarmament Brigade, to whom the rebels were supposed to hand over their arms, the army said.
"It's not convenient for the government (to report the abduction) because they don't want to risk the peace process," the army source said, explaining the government position.

Army officials said the contra rebel group that carried out the kidnapping was led by Jose Vicente Blandon, alias "El Cadejo." Unconfirmed radio reports said the group wanted one of its jailed colleagues to be freed.

The contra rebels, who were heavily backed by then-U.S. President Ronald Reagan, waged war during the 1980s on the revolutionary Sandinista government of Nicaragua. Although Nicaragua is now on its second elected non-Sandinista president, some of the former contra groups remain active in the mountainous north.
Under the terms of the May 30 agreement, the roughly 700 remaining contras were to disband by the middle of July.
